title: Native HTTP control gate for the PRIVATE315 rendered-state workload
purpose: Measure the strongest cheap source-native revalidation surface before any SeenRelay-vs-Browserbase economics claim. This experiment does not assume HTTP source validators are semantically identical to a Browserbase PNG render; it establishes whether they are a material competing shortcut that any later fit claim must defeat or distinguish from.

frozen_source_contract.initial_resource_bytes_and_sha256: measured transiently; only aggregate byte counts are retained

decision_rule.NATIVE_CONDITIONAL_SHORTCUT_STRONG: All 4 resources expose a usable conditional validator and all 80 conditional validations return HTTP 304 while source/deployment controls remain invariant.
decision_rule.NATIVE_FULL_HASH_SHORTCUT_PRESENT: At least one resource lacks a conditional validator, but every one of the 80 validations is authoritative via either 304 or a full-body SHA-256 match while source/deployment controls remain invariant.
decision_rule.NATIVE_CONTROL_NOT_CLEAN: Any validation fails, any fallback hash mismatches, or source/deployment invariance fails. No economics conclusion.

post_result_interpretation.NATIVE_CONDITIONAL_SHORTCUT_STRONG: A later economics experiment must treat this as a first-class competing shortcut. SeenRelay fit cannot be called good merely because it avoids Browserbase sessions; it must either prove materially different semantics that require renderer/environment evidence or beat the native path under the same user-relevant semantics.
post_result_interpretation.NATIVE_FULL_HASH_SHORTCUT_PRESENT: A later economics experiment must include full-source retrieval/hash as a competing baseline and account for its bytes/latency.
post_result_interpretation.NATIVE_CONTROL_NOT_CLEAN: Do not infer SeenRelay fit. Diagnose the failed native control separately if useful.

non_authorizations: No claim that HTTP source validators are automatically equivalent to exact rendered pixels.
